title: Newsletter platform migration: WordPress + MailPoet to self-hosted Ghost
context: The Harbor Ledger is an independent local-news publisher (2 editors, 1 part-time developer) with a 46,000-subscriber weekly newsletter and ~3,100 paying members. It runs WordPress + MailPoet on a single VPS that has had 4 outages during sends this year. Mission: publish reliably and keep reader relationships owned by the publication, not a platform. Agreed constraints: run cost <= $300/month; subscriber data stays exportable and under the publication's control. This plan is about to be dispatched for a 4-week build.
artifact:
# Migration plan: WordPress + MailPoet -> Ghost (self-hosted)

Owner: dev (0.5 FTE) + managing editor | 4 weeks | Cutover target: Tuesday after week 3 send

## 1. Why now
- 4 send-day outages in 2026 (Feb 3, Apr 21, Jun 9, Sep 15), each delaying the newsletter 2-6 hours; MailPoet's WP-cron sending competes with site traffic on the same PHP workers.
- Paid memberships currently run through 3 plugins (MailPoet, a membership plugin, a Stripe plugin) that each keep their own copy of the member list; reconciling them takes the managing editor ~3 hours/month.
- Ghost handles posts, newsletter, and paid members in one system with native Stripe support.

## 2. Target setup
- Ghost 5.x (MIT licensed) self-hosted via the official Docker image on a new 4 vCPU / 8 GB VPS ($48/mo, same provider and region as today). MySQL 8 on the same box, nightly encrypted dumps to object storage (30-day retention).
- Bulk newsletter delivery: Ghost uses Mailgun for bulk email. Estimated $90/mo at our volume (46k x ~4.3 sends/month).
- Stripe: existing Stripe account connected directly; no change in processor.
- Total run cost: ~$140/mo VPS + Mailgun + storage, vs $95/mo today.

## 3. Ownership and exit path
- The member list, consent records, and content live in our MySQL database on our VPS; Mailgun only receives per-send recipient batches.
- Ghost's members CSV export and JSON content export are scheduled weekly (cron, stored with the DB dumps), and we restore one export into a scratch Ghost instance in week 2 to prove it round-trips.
- If Mailgun becomes unsuitable, the exit is: disable Ghost newsletter sending and load the weekly members export into another bulk sender. In week 2 we rehearse this end to end with a 50-address internal list through Postmark Broadcasts (export -> import -> send -> unsubscribe link writes back via Ghost members API).
- Transactional mail (sign-in links, receipts) goes over plain SMTP and is provider-independent.

## 4. Subscriber migration
- Export MailPoet subscribers with status, list membership, subscribe date, and consent source/IP where recorded.
- Unsubscribed and bounced addresses are imported as suppressed (never as active), so nobody who opted out is re-mailed.
- Paid members are matched to Stripe customers by Stripe customer ID (not email) using Ghost's Stripe import; 37 members with mismatched emails were identified in a dry run and will be resolved by hand before cutover.
- Dry-run import on staging in week 1; counts reconciled against MailPoet totals (active / unsubscribed / bounced / paid) before the production import.

## 5. Content and URLs
- WordPress posts migrated with Ghost's WP exporter plugin (tested on a full staging copy: 6,812 posts, 0 failed, 41 posts with embedded shortcodes fixed by script).
- URL structure kept identical (/YYYY/MM/slug/) via Ghost routes.yaml; 301 redirects for category and tag archives. A crawl of the 2,000 most-visited URLs from analytics must return 200/301 before cutover.

## 6. Cutover and rollback
- DNS TTL lowered to 300 s one week before cutover.
- Cutover Tuesday (send day is Thursday), giving 2 days to fix issues before the first Ghost send.
- WordPress stays running read-only on the old VPS for 30 days; rollback = repoint DNS and re-enable MailPoet sending, with any new Ghost signups exported and re-imported to MailPoet.
- First Ghost send goes to a 2,000-subscriber seed segment; the remainder sends 2 hours later if bounce rate < 2% and complaint rate < 0.1%.

## 7. Timeline
- Week 1: VPS + Ghost + backups; subscriber and content dry runs on staging.
- Week 2: theme port, routes/redirects, export round-trip test, Mailgun domain warm-up (SPF/DKIM/DMARC).
- Week 3: Stripe import dry run, reconciliation, editor training; final Thursday send on MailPoet.
- Week 4: cutover Tuesday, seeded first send Thursday, 30-day read-only WP retained.

## 8. Success measures
- Zero send-day outages over the first quarter.
- Member reconciliation time for the managing editor: 3 h/month -> < 30 min/month.
decoys: Dependence on Mailgun (single bulk-email provider) looks like vendor lock-in, but §3 keeps the member list and consent records in the publication's own database, schedules weekly exports with a tested round-trip restore, and documents swapping the bulk provider via Ghost's email adapter.

Re-mailing unsubscribed readers / consent compliance during migration looks risky, but §4 imports unsubscribed and bounced addresses as suppressed, carries consent source, and reconciles counts on staging before the production import.
